title: A newborn
hook: a new person in the world: hold or picture a baby and let the newness land

segments.voice: Yesterday, the music: one piece, heard all the way through, from David's harp to Rumi's reed in the Masnavi. Did a song stop you anywhere? Today, a smaller sound. The first cry of someone new. Day one thousand forty-two.

A hospital corridor at three in the morning. Behind one door, a room that held two people an hour ago now holds three. Someone small is crying, and nobody in the room minds at all. Tiny fingers. A face nobody has seen before, anywhere, ever. A person who was not in the world yesterday, and now is. Grown-ups who were exhausted a minute ago go quiet and stare. They aren't looking at a problem to solve. They're looking at something brand new. Today's practice is that stare.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `A FACE NOBODY HAS SEEN BEFORE.` → `SOMETHING BRAND NEW.`

segments.voice: First, a mother who kept quiet. In the Gospel of Luke, shepherds come in from the fields to see a newborn lying in a manger, and they spread the word about what they had been told of this child. In the King James words: "all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The shepherds spread the news, and the hearers wonder. The mother keeps it, and ponders. Second, a poet's warning. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran's book of short teachings, a woman holding a baby asks about children. The answer begins: "Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself." Gibran goes on to say that parents may give their children love, but not their thoughts, because children have thoughts of their own. A newborn isn't a copy. It's someone new. Third, why a baby stops us. Much of what we meet in a day we've met before: the same roads, the same faces, the same news. A newborn is plain proof that the world is still making new things. Not new products. New people, with their own faces and their own thoughts to come. Fourth, the baby you once were. Not everyone has a baby to hold, and for some people the subject is tender. But whoever is listening was once that new: unknown, unnamed, brand new. The newness in that room was, once, yours.
screen: `LUKE 2: MARY PONDERED.` · `GIBRAN: LIFE'S LONGING FOR ITSELF.` · `PROOF THE WORLD STILL MAKES NEW THINGS.` · `THE BABY YOU ONCE WERE.` · then, large: `PONDERED IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: If there's a baby in your life and in your arms, hold them, and just look. If not, picture one: a child you know, a photo, or a baby you once held. Or picture yourself on your first day, small and unnamed. Look at the hands. The tiny nails. The breathing, quick and shallow. Let the newness land. If you pray, you can keep this moment the way Mary did, and ponder it. If you don't, just stay with the wonder of someone new. The bell holds the time.
A newborn. A person who wasn't in the world yesterday: something to ponder, in Luke's telling, and nobody's copy, in Gibran's. Today's word.
Your line: new. Once today, look at someone you know well, a child, a friend, a partner, as if you were seeing their face for the very first time. Day one thousand forty-two.

howItsDone: Several traditions mark a birth with blessings, naming ceremonies and prayers of thanks; Luke's account of the shepherds and Mary, and Gibran's words on children in The Prophet, are two texts that look at a new life with wonder.
